problems.original_statement: Trial eligibility is assessed at a screening visit; a database records what a clinician happened to order. Restricting an emulation to patients with complete eligibility information therefore selects on laboratory testing, clinical documentation and specialist access, which differ systematically from the excluded patients. Weighting methods for missing eligibility have recently been developed and the literature remains small. The harder version of the problem is that eligibility is latent rather than merely missing: an absent creatinine value is consistent both with a patient who would have failed the criterion and with one who was never tested, and the missingness itself may depend on treatment anticipation or on the impending outcome.
problems.correction_note: Systematic differences between the included and the excluded do not by themselves establish bias for a specified estimand; the bias arises when observation of the criterion depends on determinants of treatment or outcome that the recorded history does not control. The literature is also larger than one paper. The entry's claim that imputing the value and imputing eligibility have not been separated was too strong: they require different models, and coherent implementations of either can target the same causal estimand.
problems.statement: Trial eligibility is assessed at a screening visit; a database records what a clinician happened to order. Restricting an emulation to patients with complete eligibility information can bias it when observation of the criterion depends on determinants of treatment or outcome that the recorded history does not adequately control, which is the ordinary case when testing tracks severity and access. Weighting and missing-data methods for unrecorded eligibility now exist in more than one paper. The harder version remains: eligibility is latent rather than merely missing, since an absent creatinine value is consistent both with a patient who would have failed the criterion and with one who was never tested. When true eligibility among unobserved records is missing not at random, the effect in the truly eligible population is not identified from the main data alone and requires either additional identifying assumptions or external information.
problems.why_open: Missing-at-random conditional on the recorded history is not credible here, because the recording decision is a clinical judgment informed by the same severity that predicts the outcome. The external information that would identify the effect is a validation source in which the criterion was assessed for everyone, and such sources are rare, rarely representative, and rarely transportable to the analysis population. Imputing the underlying measurement and imputing the eligibility indicator need different models, so an implementation has to choose which object it is modeling and defend that choice, and applied work seldom states which it did.
problems.proposed_direction: Model true eligibility and its observation jointly, anchoring the measurement model on validation records where the criterion was assessed for everyone. Compare multiple imputation, inverse-probability-of-eligibility weighting, doubly robust selection correction and partial-identification bounds on the same data, stating for each whether the model is of the measurement or of the eligibility indicator, since they are not interchangeable even when they target the same estimand. Report the eligible population under each approach alongside the effect, because a method that changes who is in the trial has changed the estimand.

prior_work.cite: Benz L, et al. Adjusting for selection bias due to missing eligibility criteria in emulated target trials. Am J Epidemiol 2025
prior_work.what_it_does: Develops weighting for missing eligibility information in emulated trials.

prior_work.what_it_does: A second direct treatment of the problem, for survival outcomes in record data.

problems.original_statement: An eligibility criterion is a conditioning statement, and conditioning on a variable that is a common effect of treatment and outcome opens a path rather than closing one. Emulation protocols routinely build eligibility from healthcare-use variables such as a required prior visit, a recorded baseline laboratory value or a minimum enrollment period, all of which can be descendants of the treatment decision or of early disease. Nothing in the current workflow checks an eligibility definition for this property, and the reporting checklist asks what the criteria were rather than what conditioning on them does.
problems.correction_note: The timing in the original was wrong. Eligibility is fixed before the time-zero treatment, so it cannot be a descendant of the treatment under study. The mechanism that does operate runs through pre-baseline treatment decisions, incipient disease and common causes of care-seeking and outcome, and it produces selection bias when the criterion is a collider or a descendant of one in the assumed graph. Being a healthcare-use variable is not by itself sufficient.
problems.statement: An eligibility criterion is a conditioning statement, and conditioning on a variable that is a collider, or a relevant descendant of one, in the graph relating determinants of treatment and outcome opens a noncausal path rather than closing one. Emulation protocols routinely build eligibility from healthcare-use variables: a required prior visit, a recorded baseline laboratory value, a minimum enrollment period. Being a healthcare-use variable is not sufficient for the bias, and these variables are the ones most likely to sit at the junction, because pre-baseline treatment decisions, incipient disease and the common causes of care-seeking and outcome all feed them. Nothing in the current workflow checks an eligibility definition for that structure before the analysis runs, and the reporting checklist asks what the criteria were rather than what conditioning on them does.
problems.why_open: Whether a criterion is a collider depends on the causal structure, which is what the study is trying to learn, so the check cannot be purely empirical. Observational data alone cannot certify the required structure: graph-learning algorithms recover a Markov equivalence class at best and are further limited by latent confounding, so they can flag candidates and never license removal. Removing a criterion also changes the target population, so the correction carries a cost that has to be argued clinically rather than statistically, and domain-grounded causal review therefore remains necessary rather than replaceable.
problems.proposed_direction: Build a causal-discovery eligibility auditor that combines temporal checks with graph learning under explicit assumptions, flagging criteria that are post-baseline, that are colliders, or that encode healthcare use, and treat its output as advisory input to a domain review rather than as an automatic exclusion. Evaluate it on generated graphs with known structure, scoring collider-warning sensitivity, false-positive rate, expert agreement and, decisively, whether acting on the warnings reduces bias. Never let an algorithm define eligibility by maximizing the apparent treatment effect, which is a search over estimands dressed as a design step.
